meta.title: Natural Resources and Their Use
meta.source: NCERT Grade 8, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 1

sections.title: 1. When does Nature become a Resource?
points: Nature is the totality of life and non-life forms in our environment that humans did not create.
'Natural resources' are materials and substances that occur in Nature and are valuable to humans.
An element of Nature becomes a resource when humans use it for sustenance or make new things from it.
Trees exist independently of humans, but become a resource when their wood is used for furniture.
For an entity to be called a resource, it should be technologically accessible, economically feasible to exploit and culturally acceptable.
Petroleum deep under the ocean may remain a non-resource if technology cannot reach it or extraction costs too much.
Cutting trees in sacred groves may be culturally unacceptable even when the wood is valuable.
In this chapter, 'exploitation' simply means extraction, utilisation and consumption of natural resources.

sections.title: 2. Categories of Natural Resources
points: Categorisation uses shared characteristics and names so that ideas can be discussed and communicated efficiently.
One way to group natural resources is by the uses we put them to.
Resources essential for life include the air we breathe, the water we drink and the food we eat.
Humans cannot make the air, water or soil on which life depends; these are taken from the atmosphere, rivers, ponds and cultivated soil.
Resources for materials include wood, marble, coal and gold, used for utility or to create things of beauty.
Resources for energy include coal, water, petroleum, natural gas, sunlight and wind.
Energy is a cornerstone of modern living: it powers buildings, transport and production processes.

sections.title: 3. Renewable resources and Nature's cycles
points: Nature functions in a restorative and regenerative way.
Restoration is the process of returning something degraded or damaged to its original healthy state.
Regeneration goes beyond restoration: it is Nature's ability to create new life and the conditions for thriving.
A cut on the skin healing and a forest recovering after a wildfire are examples of restoration.
Planting the types of trees that originally grew in an area restores the ecosystem and enables life to return.
In a forest, a fallen tree decomposes and enriches the soil; new trees grow from seeds and the cycle continues.
Renewable resources include solar energy, wind energy, energy from flowing water, timber from forests, rivers fed by rain and glaciers, and soil that replenishes itself.
Renewable resources stay renewable only if the natural rhythm of restoration and regeneration is not disturbed.
Harvesting timber faster than a forest can grow trees will eventually deplete the forest.
Fossil-fuel-driven industrialisation and the cutting down of forests have disturbed Nature's cycles and contributed to rising temperatures.
Some Himalayan glaciers are melting faster than precipitation can replace them, threatening water security for people in the plains.

sections.title: 4. Non-renewable resources
points: Non-renewable resources are created over long periods and cannot be replenished at the rate we use them.
Fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum are non-renewable, as are minerals and metals such as iron, copper and gold.
India has significant coal reserves, but estimates suggest they may last only about another 50 years.
Rising population and accelerating development are increasing the demand for electricity.
Coal must be used judiciously until more sustainable options become widely available.

sections.title: 5. Ecosystem functions and services
points: Ecosystem functions are Nature's inherent ways of working, such as trees producing oxygen or forests filtering water.
Ecosystem services are the benefits humans receive when those natural processes work in their favour.
A forest's functions include filtering water, preventing soil erosion and providing habitat for animals.
People receive ecosystem services in the form of clean water, protected farmland and pollinated crops.
A mature tree produces about 275 litres of oxygen a day, while a human being needs about 350 litres a day; both figures vary.
Industrial waste discharged untreated into rivers can exceed Nature's capacity to recycle it, making the water poisonous and unable to support life.
Traditional communities regulated or refrained from fishing during the spawning season to maintain fish populations.
Commercialisation of fishing led to over-fishing; tuna populations, for example, declined sharply despite later agreements to control fishing.

topics.topic: Distribution and the Paradox of Plenty

sections.title: 6. Uneven distribution and its implications
points: Natural resources are not evenly distributed across the planet or even within countries.
Uneven distribution shapes human settlements, trade patterns, international relations and conflicts.
Many wars have been fought, and continue to be fought, to gain control over natural resources.
Industries located near natural resources create employment for local people and allow townships to grow.
More modern facilities that improve the quality of life often become accessible around resource industries.
These benefits come with short-term and long-term costs, including the displacement of people from resource-rich areas.
In some cases sacred places are threatened by extraction, leading to conflict.
Trade depends on the geographical location of resources; combined with human knowledge and skills, resources create unique products such as Wootz steel.
Trade in resources fuelled the development of large empires in India.

sections.title: 7. Shared resources and conflict
points: Nature does not pay attention to political boundaries, which creates tensions over sharing resources between states and countries.
The Kaveri river water is shared among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry.
Negotiation and deft management were required to maintain peace and fair sharing of the Kaveri waters.
Reaching agreements between neighbouring countries over shared resources is especially difficult.
The Brahmaputra is an example of waters shared across international borders.

sections.title: 8. The 'Paradox of Plenty'
points: Having abundant natural resources does not guarantee economic prosperity.
Some resource-rich regions experience slower economic growth and development.
Economists call this the 'natural resource curse' or the 'paradox of plenty'.
A common reason is the failure to develop industries that convert resources into products of higher value.
India has generally avoided the resource curse by investing in industries that meet its growing needs.
The challenge of balancing resource extraction with sustainability remains.

sections.title: 9. From resources to lasting benefits
points: Understanding and managing natural resources is a valuable starting point, but it is not enough.
Human knowledge, good governance and strategic planning determine whether resources become lasting benefits or temporary windfalls.
Investments in technology and skills can help overcome the resource curse.

sections.title: 10. Groundwater and soil
points: Many farmers extract groundwater for irrigation faster than the water table is replenished.
The deficit raises the cost of extraction and can eventually make groundwater unavailable.
It has been predicted that many growing cities will run out of groundwater soon.
Remedies include traditional water harvesting, rejuvenating ponds and tanks, cutting wasteful consumption, and processing and reusing water.
Improper use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides has led to soil degradation.
Traditional practices such as cow dung and natural fertilisers, mulching and multi-cropping supported holistic soil management.
We must learn from these practices, replenish the soil and rejuvenate it to prevent further degradation.

sections.title: 11. Overexploitation of groundwater: the Punjab caselet
points: Punjab was home to the Green Revolution, which fed a large share of India's population and helped the country become self-sufficient in food.
In the 1960s, farmers shifted to high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy that required more water than traditional seeds.
Free power encouraged the over-pumping of groundwater, a situation still prevalent in much of India.
Modern farming techniques also required chemical pesticides and fertilisers.
Groundwater in much of Punjab is now inaccessible to depths of about 30 metres.
Chemicals from pesticides and fertilisers have dissolved in the groundwater, causing health hazards.
Almost 80% of Punjab's area has been classified as 'over-exploited', meaning water is drawn faster than it can be restored.
Food security was ensured in the short term, but the long-term damage will take time and effort to heal.

sections.title: 12. The case of cement
points: Cement is essential for houses, schools, hospitals, bridges, roads and airports.
Cement production is listed as one of the most polluting industries.
Fine dust from cement production damages human and animal lungs, settles on leaves and reduces plant yields, and pollutes soil and water.
The Central Pollution Control Board has created guidelines for cement factories to minimise or eliminate pollution.
Alternatives include traditional materials such as stone and mud, new plant-based materials, and recycled materials from waste plastic.
Combining traditional materials and methods with modern technology can produce sustainable materials that pollute less, provide local employment and suit the local climate.

sections.title: 13. Vrikshayurveda: traditional plant science
points: Vrikshayurveda is an ancient Indian botanical science focused on the study and care of plants and trees.
'Vriksha' means tree and 'ayurveda' means the science of life or health.
The knowledge system dates back several millennia and was formalised in texts such as Surapala's Vrikshayurveda around the 10th century CE.
It recommends specific plants for different soil types and gives methods for seed collection, preservation and pre-planting treatment.
It describes irrigation according to plant species, growth stage and season.
It recommends pest management through natural repellents and companion planting, and promotes crop rotation and mixed cropping for soil health.
It advises ploughing methods that retain soil moisture and support soil organisms such as fungi, bacteria and earthworms.

sections.title: 14. A caselet from Sikkim
points: Pema's family farm in Sikkim faced declining yields and mounting debts from expensive chemical inputs.
When the state government announced a policy to promote organic farming, the family decided to try it.
The transition was difficult: yields initially dropped while the soil recovered from years of chemical use.
The family switched to compost, natural pest repellents made from neem and garlic, and multiple crops across the year.
After about five years the farm was thriving, selling cardamom, ginger and traditional vegetables at premium prices.
In 2016 Sikkim became a 100 per cent organic state, with all of its farmland certified organic.
Local biodiversity flourished, beneficial insects and birds returned, tourism increased and farmers' incomes grew by 20 per cent on average.

sections.title: 15. Judicious use, solar energy and equity
points: For non-renewable resources, we must use them so that they last long enough for humanity to find more sustainable alternatives.
We need to switch to renewable sources of energy for as many purposes as possible.
India and France launched the International Alliance for Solar Energy (IASE) in 2015, a coalition of sunshine-rich countries committed to harnessing solar power.
India has helped channel billions of dollars into solar projects across developing nations, sharing technical expertise and creating affordable financing options.
The Bhadla Solar Park symbolises India's solar ambitions and its transition from traditional energy sources to renewables.
For Indians, the International Solar Alliance represents both environmental responsibility and economic opportunity.
Distribution of and access to resources, including water and clean air, is often unfair to some sections of society.
Many city areas lack an adequate and regular supply of drinking water, and air pollution affects those least able to protect themselves.
The Bhagavad Gita's idea of lokasangraha calls on everyone to transcend personal desires and act for the wellbeing of all.
We must act as stewards of natural resources, working toward restoration, regeneration and sustainability.
